title: Privacy, security and engineering
intro: Everyday Dental is a fictional portfolio demonstration. Clinical services, real patient accounts, payments, email and SMS are disabled. A sample patient journey runs in memory in your browser. It does not create a real medical record.

sections.title: What this website processes
sections.text: The application uses no advertising, analytics or session replay scripts. Stock images are served from this site; no map is embedded. Your language preference may be stored locally. Sample workflow changes and activity are kept only in this tab’s memory. Hosting and network providers necessarily receive network metadata such as an IP address to deliver and protect the site. Their operational processing is separate from the synthetic patient example.

sections.title: Your choices
sections.text: You can clear the language preference below, reset the sample journey, or close the tab. Optional sharing starts off and can be changed in the sample. No information is sold or shared for advertising by the application; a Global Privacy Control signal does not enable any tracking. An actual clinic must provide verified contact and rights-request channels before launch.

sections.title: US and EU legal scope
sections.text: The accompanying report covers HIPAA applicability, FTC health-breach rules, California and Washington examples, GDPR, ePrivacy and accessibility. Software controls alone do not establish compliance. Real clinics need applicable contracts, risk assessments, staffing, retention rules and jurisdiction-specific advice. No HIPAA, GDPR or SOC 2 certification is claimed.

sections.title: Security boundary
sections.text: The deployed demonstration is static, with no clinical database connection or write API. Real intake forms are read-only previews. The sample role selector illustrates access decisions; it is not authentication or a server authorization system. Strict browser security headers, first-party assets and no persistent patient storage reduce the exposed surface. Original clinical prototypes require separate remediation and verification before use.

sections.title: Accessibility
sections.text: The review pages support keyboard controls, visible focus, a skip link, responsive text and announced workflow results. Reduced-motion preferences are respected. Automated tests are limited evidence; a full assistive-technology and disabled-user review is required before claiming WCAG conformance. Demonstration figures, reviews, pricing and clinician profiles are illustrative, not verified clinical outcomes.

sections.title: 10,000 to 1,000,000 simultaneous users
sections.text: These are architecture planning scenarios, not measured capacity. Public pages can be delivered through a CDN without a database request per reader. Active clinical transactions need authenticated stateless APIs, bounded database pools, indexed tenant-scoped queries, queues and multiple failure domains. The engineering plan provides request-rate calculations, staged acceptance gates and a cost-approval boundary.

sections.title: 99% availability target
sections.text: A 99% time-based target permits 432 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month. This is a target, not an observed service level or contractual SLA. A single shared server is a failure domain. Restore tests, external probes, incident ownership and sustained observation are necessary; multi-region failover requires separately funded infrastructure.

sections.title: Research and release evidence
sections.text: The repository includes the legal research, threat model, clinical release blockers, scaling design, reproducible tests and operational runbooks. Read the verification report for exact checks and limits. The public demo must never be used for emergencies, treatment, real patient records or payments.
